konflikt-v-iranu-a-ceny-paliv-proc-benzi.title: Conflict in Iran and fuel prices: Why petrol and diesel are going up and what comes next
konflikt-v-iranu-a-ceny-paliv-proc-benzi.seoDescription: Find out why the Iran conflict is pushing up petrol and diesel prices in the Czech Republic, how the Strait of Hormuz affects them and what to expect in 2026.
konflikt-v-iranu-a-ceny-paliv-proc-benzi.content:
Tension in the Middle East has shaken up world markets once again, and this time it isn’t just a distant geopolitical problem playing out somewhere “far away”. The conflict around Iran is feeding very quickly into the everyday reality of ordinary people. A single glance at the prices at fuel stations makes it clear that global events have a direct impact on our wallets.
The year 2026 is bringing a renewed rise in petrol and diesel prices. One of the main triggers is the situation around Iran and the strategically vital Strait of Hormuz, a place that acts as the “artery of the world’s oil”.
How exactly does this conflict affect fuel prices? Why are prices rising even without a real oil shortage? And what can we expect in the coming months? Let’s break it down step by step.
## Why Iran has such a major influence on fuel prices
Iran isn’t just another oil state; it is a player whose influence reaches far beyond oil production itself. It is one of the world’s largest oil producers and also occupies a strategic position that gives it enormous geopolitical power.
Interestingly, even though sanctions often stop Iran from using its full export potential, its importance to the markets doesn’t diminish. Why? It controls an area that global oil supplies practically cannot do without.
### The Strait of Hormuz as a critical point
When it comes to energy, the Strait of Hormuz is one of the most important places on the planet. Every day, it carries roughly:
- 20 to 30% of all the world’s oil
- huge volumes of liquefied natural gas (LNG)
- thousands of tankers a year
It is a narrow sea corridor between Iran and Oman, and it is precisely its vulnerability that makes it “the world’s most expensive bottleneck”.
As soon as there is a threat of:
- restrictions on shipping
- military tension
- or even a blockade
markets react almost instantly. And they do so even if the strait never actually closes.
Worth knowing: A mere statement or a military exercise in the region is enough to make the oil price jump by several per cent within hours.
The result? A rapid rise in oil prices that feeds through to fuel prices almost immediately.
## How the conflict in Iran is making petrol and diesel more expensive
At first glance, it might seem that a conflict thousands of kilometres away shouldn’t have such a rapid impact. In reality, though, the whole process is very straightforward and, above all, fast.
### Market jitters
Investors and oil traders follow the situation literally in real time. As soon as there is a risk of supply disruption, they start “hedging their positions”, in other words buying oil earlier and at higher prices.
It’s not just about reality, but about expectations. The fear of a shortage often has a stronger effect than the shortage itself.
### The rising price of Brent crude
Brent crude, which is key for Europe, is highly sensitive to geopolitical tension.
There is one important thing to understand: The price of oil can rise even without any actual cut in production.
All it takes is:
- increased risk
- speculation
- or uncertainty about the future
And the price shoots up.
### Rising fuel prices in Europe
As soon as the oil price rises, refineries and distributors react. They pay more for the raw material and so, logically, raise the prices of the end products.
Other factors also feed into fuel prices:
- the dollar exchange rate
- transport costs
- distributors’ margins
- taxes
This means that even a relatively small movement in the oil price can mean a noticeable increase at the pump.
### The impact on drivers
At the end of the whole chain is the ordinary driver.
They will feel:
- higher petrol and diesel prices
- more expensive transport
- rising prices of goods (because of logistics)
In other words: expensive oil doesn’t just make filling up dearer, it gradually makes life as a whole more expensive.
## Fuel price forecast: What to expect in the coming months
The future of fuel prices is always a combination of economics, politics and psychology. And the conflict in Iran adds a hefty dose of uncertainty to the mix.
### Escalation of the conflict
If the situation came to a head:
- oil prices could spike sharply
- markets would react with panic
- there could be short-term market shocks
In an extreme scenario, prices could reach levels we saw during major crises.
### The situation stabilises
If the situation calms down:
- price growth will slow
- markets will “catch their breath”
- prices may fall slightly
But a return to significantly lower levels tends to be slow.
### Long-term tension
The most likely scenario for 2026:
- fluctuating prices
- frequent swings
- long-term uncertainty
Businesses and households alike therefore have to reckon with the fact that stable, cheap fuel can no longer be taken for granted.
## Why prices sometimes rise faster than makes sense
This is the point where most people think: “Surely this can’t just be down to the conflict.”
And they are partly right.
### Market psychology
Markets aren’t just about numbers; they are about emotions.
Prices react to:
- expectations about the future
- media reports
- investor speculation
This means prices can rise “in advance”, before anything has actually happened.
Example: If the market expects a problem in a month’s time, the oil price rises today.
## Conspiracy theories vs reality
Whenever prices rise, all sorts of theories pop up. Some sound logical, others less so.
### The most common claims
- oil companies are artificially inflating prices
- conflicts are orchestrated for profit
- prices are being manipulated for no reason
These views are popular mainly because they offer a simple explanation for a complex problem.
### What the reality is
The truth is more complex.
Oil prices are influenced by a combination of factors:
- global supply and demand
- geopolitical tension
- decisions by major producers
- financial markets and speculation
Yes, some movements may be exaggerated. But in most cases the underlying reasons for rising prices are real.
## How to protect yourself against rising fuel prices
And now for the most practical part: what ordinary people can do about it.
Rising fuel prices are forcing drivers to look for ways to save. And this is exactly where a new trend of “active refuelling” is emerging.
More and more often, people are looking for:
- petrol and diesel discounts
- cheaper fuel stations
- cashback schemes
- loyalty apps
## Smart refuelling as a response to expensive fuel
In 2026 it’s no longer enough to just “fill up wherever is on the way”.
Smart refuelling means:
- tracking prices in real time
- planning your fill-ups
- making use of discounts and rewards
- combining different money-saving strategies
Worth knowing: The difference between the cheapest and the most expensive pump can easily be several crowns per litre, which adds up to hundreds of crowns on a full tank.
So it’s not just about saving money, but about changing your approach.
## Summary: A distant conflict, an impact close to home
The situation in Iran is a textbook example of how interconnected today’s world is.
A conflict thousands of kilometres away:
- affects fuel prices in Europe
- makes transport and goods more expensive
- reaches into everyday life
And that is exactly why fuel prices are among the key issues of 2026.
One thing is certain:
uncertainty is here to stay, and the ability to adapt will become more and more important.

kvalitni-palivo-vs-nizka-cena-musite-se-.title: Quality fuel vs. low price: Should you be afraid of cheap fill-ups?
kvalitni-palivo-vs-nizka-cena-musite-se-.seoDescription: Worried about cheap petrol and diesel? Find out how the Czech Trade Inspection Authority (ČOI) checks fuel quality and why a low price doesn’t mean bad fuel.
kvalitni-palivo-vs-nizka-cena-musite-se-.content:
It circulates among drivers like a bogeyman: “Fill up with cheap diesel and you’ll wreck your injectors.” This myth often keeps prices high at the big chains, while smaller stations offer fuel of the same quality for much fairer money. But what is the truth? Does a low price necessarily come at the cost of risk to your engine, or are you simply paying for the brand and the premium coffee in the shop? We looked at how quality checks work in the Czech Republic and why, with the PHMarket app, you can fill up cheaply with a clear conscience.
#### 1. The myth of “bad” cheap petrol, and whether it is really quality fuel
#### 2. Who keeps an eye on what comes out of the nozzle?
#### 3. So why are prices at some stations so much lower?
#### 4. Additives: The real difference between “standard” and “premium”
#### 5. How PHMarket filters reliable partners
#### 6. Tips to avoid a bad fill-up
### 1. The myth of “bad” cheap petrol, and whether it is really quality fuel
For years, Czech drivers have passed around one dangerous equation: low price = risk to the engine. This idea often dates back to the 1990s, when the fuel market was like the Wild West and quality fluctuated. Today, however, the situation is completely different. Even so, many motorists are still afraid to leave the motorway for a lesser-known fuel station, even if it would mean saving several hundred CZK on a single tank.
#### The psychology of the price board: Why do we trust a higher price?
It is a classic psychological effect. We have a subconscious feeling that if a litre of petrol costs 3 CZK more, there must be “something extra” in it. The big multinational chains invest millions of CZK in marketing to build this feeling. They sell you a sense of safety, luxurious facilities and premium coffee. Yet the fuel in their tanks often comes from the same distribution depot (e.g. Čepro) as the fuel at a small family-run station a few kilometres down the road.
#### Facts vs. impressions
All fuels sold on the Czech market must, without exception, meet the strict national standards ČSN EN 228 (for petrol) and ČSN EN 590 (for diesel). If a fuel failed to meet these standards, the station would risk crippling fines from the Czech Trade Inspection Authority (ČOI) and an immediate ban on sales. So the difference between fuel at 35 CZK and fuel at 39 CZK usually lies not in its basic composition, but in the cost of the brand, the retailer’s margin and the extra services you get at the pump.
### 2. Who keeps an eye on what comes out of the nozzle?
Many drivers live in fear that quality checks happen once a year and that in the meantime the station owner can do whatever they like with the fuel. The opposite is true. The fuel inspection system in the Czech Republic is one of the strictest in Europe, which is great news for users of apps like PHMarket.
#### The role of the ČOI: The guardian of your tank
The main body that watches over fuel purity is the Czech Trade Inspection Authority (ČOI). Its inspectors take unannounced samples all over the country, from busy motorway routes to small village stations. They monitor key parameters such as the flash point, sulphur content and the presence of bio components. The results of these inspections are public, and for every fuel station they are a huge deterrent. If the fuel fails, an immediate sales ban follows, together with a fine that can put smaller operators out of business.
#### The Quality Seal as a guide
Besides state inspection, there are also voluntary certifications, such as the “Quality Seal” (Pečeť kvality) programme. Fuel stations that take part in this scheme have their samples regularly tested in independent laboratories (e.g. SGS). So if you see the relevant sticker at the pump, you can be sure that the retailer goes beyond its legal obligations to prove that its fuel is in perfect condition.
#### Transparency in the digital age
Thanks to digitalisation and projects such as PHMarket, information about wrongdoing spreads faster than ever before. Nowadays no reputable retailer can afford to risk its reputation for a short-term profit from poor-quality fuel. The community of drivers and instant feedback act as another natural filter that pushes dishonest operators out of the market.
### 3. So why are prices at some stations so much lower?
If we already know that quality is policed by the state and the standards are the same for everyone, one last mystery remains: pricing. Why does the price board on one side of the road show 39.90 CZK and, a few kilometres further on, 35.50 CZK? Don’t look for the answer in the tank, but in operating costs and business strategy.
#### Operating costs: Automated vs. full-service
The price difference is often determined by what you see around the pump. A large fuel station that is open around the clock, with a car wash, a heated shop and staff who will make you a coffee, has enormous overheads. These costs, from energy to wages, have to be paid by someone. And that someone is the driver, in the price of every litre. At the other end of the scale are self-service (automated) stations or smaller stations with minimal facilities. Their operating costs are a fraction of that, which allows them to lower their prices without losing profit.
#### Business strategy: Margin as a choice
For the big chains, fuel is often just one of many products, and their margins are set to satisfy shareholders and pay for costly marketing campaigns. Smaller retailers or networks working with PHMarket often choose the opposite strategy: low margin, high volume. Rather than earning 5 CZK per litre from ten drivers, they prefer to earn 1 CZK per litre from a hundred drivers, brought to them by the app and a good reputation.
#### Logistics and location
The price is also affected by how far the tanker has to travel from the depot (e.g. from the Čepro terminals) and how expensive the land lease is. A station at a motorway exit pays astronomical sums for its location, which naturally feed through into the final price. Local stations in industrial zones or on the outskirts of towns don’t have to pay these “location surcharges”.
### 4. Additives: The real difference between “standard” and “premium”
While the base petrol or diesel is practically identical at most stations, what turns it into a “test winner” is additives. These are special chemical blends added to fuel to clean the engine, reduce friction and protect the fuel system against corrosion.
#### What does your engine really have an appetite for?
Modern direct-injection engines are sensitive to cleanliness. If you fill up with fuel without additives over the long term, carbon deposits can build up in the engine. Good-quality fuel with additives dissolves these deposits and keeps the engine in good shape. But does that mean you have to buy the most expensive “premium” diesel at the motorway? Not necessarily.
#### Premium fuel for a fraction of the price
Many cheaper fuel stations now add additives as standard (they often say so right on the pump). But if you come across a station with an extremely low price that doesn’t use additives, you have two options:
1. Add your own: Many experienced drivers buy their own additives in a can (e.g. the well-known VIF). By adding a small amount to the tank, you create fuel that outperforms even expensive premium brands, at a cost of just a fraction of a crown per litre.
1. Choose smartly in the app: PHMarket helps you find stations that offer fuel with additives at fair prices, so you don’t have to mix anything yourself, wearing gloves in the car park.
#### Are premium fuels just marketing?
With high-octane petrol (100+) or special bio-free winter diesels, “premium” does make sense, especially in sports cars or in frosts below -20 °C. For the everyday running of a family car, though, long-term cleanliness is what matters most. And that can be ensured just as well by cheaper fuel with additives from an honest retailer, which you will find on the PHMarket map.
### 5. How PHMarket filters reliable partners
You may be thinking: “Fine, the prices are great and the standards are strict, but how am I supposed to know that this particular cheap station in the industrial zone is all right?” This is exactly where PHMarket comes in. Our goal is not just to show the lowest number on the map, but to connect drivers with retailers who play fair.
#### Station selection: No “dodgy” backyard operations
Not everyone gets into the PHMarket partner station network. We look into retailers’ track records and focus on those with stable operations and a transparent fuel origin. So in the app you won’t find any makeshift tanks in fields, only vetted fuel stations that meet all legal requirements and often go well beyond them.
#### Transparency and community
The digital age puts enormous power into drivers’ hands. If any of the stations in our network started showing problems with quality or substandard service, our feedback system and data monitoring would alert us immediately. Transparency is our priority: if a station isn’t good enough for our users, it has no place in the app.
#### Long-term stability instead of one-off swings
We track price trends and the stability of individual stations. Our partners understand that working with PHMarket is not about “lure them in and rip them off” but about building a community of satisfied drivers who will keep coming back thanks to fair prices and guaranteed quality. When you see a station in the app, you know it has made it through our screening.
### 6. Tips to avoid a bad fill-up
Even though PHMarket and state inspections protect you, it pays to know a few basic common-sense rules used by experienced drivers and professional fuel testers alike. Fuel quality depends not only on what the tanker delivered into the tank, but also on how the station owner looks after the tanks.
#### Watch the turnover: Where there’s a queue, the fuel is fresh
Fuel is a consumable and it can “age” in underground tanks, especially if it contains bio components that absorb moisture. The best guarantee of quality is therefore high turnover. If you see cars lining up at a station (even a cheap one) and people filling up there regularly, it is a clear sign that the fuel doesn’t have time to “go off” in the tanks and is constantly topped up with fresh deliveries.
#### The look of the station tells you more than you think
There doesn’t have to be a marble floor, but pay attention to how clean the pumps are. If the nozzles are greasy, there are puddles by the pumps and the surroundings look neglected, it says a lot about the owner’s approach to maintenance. An operator who keeps the forecourt clean is very likely to be just as conscientious about draining sludge from the tanks and regularly replacing the filters in the pumps.
#### When should you be on your guard?
If you come across a price that is suspiciously low even by PHMarket standards (e.g. 5 CZK lower than at other cheap stations nearby), it is worth checking whether it is an established brand or an automated station. Extreme swings that are out of line with the market can be a warning sign, but we monitor such extremes closely in our app.
Conclusion: Quality fuelling is not about how much money you leave at the till, but about the information you have in your pocket. In 2026, the fear of cheap petrol is a thing of the past: with modern inspections and tools like PHMarket, you can save thousands of CZK a year without a single worry about your engine.
Downloaded it yet? Don’t pay more for fuel than you have to. Take a look at the PHMarket map and find your nearest vetted station today.

nafta-bez-bioslozky-co-to-vlastne-znamen.title: Bio-free diesel: What does it actually mean and why all the fuss?
nafta-bez-bioslozky-co-to-vlastne-znamen.seoDescription: Bio-free diesel (B0) protects your engine from bio sludge and clogged injectors. Learn the difference between B7 and B0 and find pure diesel with PHMarket.
nafta-bez-bioslozky-co-to-vlastne-znamen.content:
MEŘO, or simply “rapeseed”. To some it is an environmental standard, to others a nightmare lurking in the fuel tank. “Bio-free diesel” is one of the most searched-for terms among Czech drivers, and for good reason. While standard diesel at the pump contains a mandatory share of bio components, which can degrade and clog up the engine when a vehicle stands unused for a long time, “pure” diesel is a blessing for the sensitive systems of modern cars. In this article we look at what the bio component in fuel really does, why your engine does (or doesn’t) like it, and how PHMarket helps you find a station where nothing but honest fuel goes into your tank.
1. What exactly is this bio component? (Basic chemistry at the pump)
- The difference between fossil diesel and MEŘO (rapeseed methyl ester).
- Why is it added to fuel at all? (Legislation and ecology).
2. The problem called “bio sludge”: Why does the engine suffer?
- Properties of the bio component: Water absorption, degradation over time and the formation of slimy deposits.
- What happens to the injectors and the pump when a car stands unused for a long time (seasonal machinery, classic cars, the family’s second car).
3. Bio-free diesel: The holy grail for modern diesels
- Advantages of “pure” diesel: Longer storage life and a lower risk of corrosion in the fuel system.
- Why it is ideal for winter and for cars with a diesel particulate filter (DPF).
4. Where does this kind of diesel come from?
- It is not a myth: there are stations that legally offer it (an explanation of the role of the state material reserves and specific retailers).
- How can you tell at the pump what you are filling up with? (B7 vs. B0 codes).
5. How do you find “pure” fuel in seconds with PHMarket?
- Using the filters in the app to search for stations with premium bio-free fuel.
- Price comparison: Is it worth paying extra for peace of mind and a clean engine?
### Chapter 1: What exactly is this bio component? (Basic chemistry at the pump)
Pull up at a fuel station today and you will see a small square label marked B7 on the diesel pump. It is not a random designation: the letter “B” stands for biodiesel and the number 7 for the percentage of bio component the fuel may contain. But what is actually hidden behind this name, and why is there so much debate about it?
#### MEŘO: Rapeseed in your tank
In the Czech Republic, the bio component in diesel is most often MEŘO (rapeseed methyl ester). It is a fuel made from vegetable oils through a process called transesterification. At first glance it sounds green and logical: we replace part of the fossil diesel, which has to be extracted and imported, with something that grows in the fields on our doorstep.
#### Why is it added to fuel at all?
The reason is not technical (as if it helped engines) but purely legislative. Both the European Union and the Czech state require fuel retailers to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Adding a bio component is the easiest way to meet the environmental limits on paper. Retailers are therefore required by law to blend the bio component into standard diesel, otherwise they would face huge fines.
#### The difference between fossil diesel and the bio component
Pure fossil diesel is a product of crude oil refining and is chemically very stable. The bio component (MEŘO), on the other hand, is of organic origin, which brings specific properties with it. It does have good lubricity, which is great for injection pumps, but it has one major drawback: it deteriorates much faster. While crude oil lasted millions of years underground, rapeseed ester in your tank starts to change its properties after just a few weeks.
### Chapter 2: The problem called “bio sludge”: Why does the engine suffer?
The bio component in diesel (MEŘO) has one property that conventional fossil diesel does not: it is hygroscopic. That is the technical term for the fact that it literally “attracts” moisture from the air. And this is exactly where a chain of problems begins that can end in an expensive trip to the garage.
#### Water in the tank and corrosion
Once the bio component has absorbed water, it stops being a stable fuel. Water in the fuel system is public enemy number one for high-pressure pumps and injectors. These components work with extreme precision and microscopic tolerances. Even a small amount of condensed water can cause corrosion or break down the lubricating film, which leads to expensive components seizing.
#### Degradation and the formation of “slime”
While pure diesel will sit in a tank for months without batting an eyelid, diesel with a bio component starts to degrade chemically after 3 to 4 months (sometimes even sooner, depending on the temperature). The organic components oxidise and form sticky, resinous deposits, in layman’s terms bio sludge. These deposits look like brown slime or jelly, which can reliably:
- Clog the fine strainer of the fuel pump.
- Block the fuel filter.
- Gum up the injector nozzles, leading to rough running, higher consumption and a loss of power.
#### The problem of “weekend” cars and seasonal machinery
Cars that are not driven every day suffer the most. If you have a car you only take out once a fortnight, or you own a classic car, a motorhome or garden machinery, the bio component in the tank is a ticking time bomb for you. During long periods of standing, bio sludge has ideal conditions to form and settle at the bottom of the tank.
### Chapter 3: Bio-free diesel: The holy grail for modern diesels
If you avoid the bio component, you get rid of 90% of the problems described in the previous chapter. Bio-free diesel (technically pure mineral diesel) is a fuel that is stable, clean and predictable. Why would you want it, even if your car is driven every day?
#### Exceptional storage life
Its biggest advantage is that it stands the test of time. Pure bio-free diesel will easily keep unchanged in a tank or a jerry can for several years. That makes it the ideal choice for:
- Classic and seasonal cars: Laid up in the garage over the winter.
- Standby generators: Where the fuel waits months for its moment.
- The family’s second car: Covering just a few kilometres a week.
#### Cleaner combustion and DPF protection
Modern diesels are fitted with a diesel particulate filter (DPF). It traps soot and then burns it off (regeneration). Bio components tend to produce slightly more ash and deposits during combustion, which clog the filter faster. Pure diesel burns “smoothly” and cleanly, which extends the life of the DPF, a part that costs tens of thousands of CZK to replace.
#### Peace of mind in winter
In winter, bio-free diesel naturally has better low-temperature properties. This is because the bio component solidifies sooner in freezing temperatures and forms paraffin crystals that clog the fuel filter. If you fill up with pure diesel, you can be far more confident of starting even on a freezing morning in the Beskids or in the mountains, without having to add litres of expensive “winter” additives.
### Chapter 4: How can you tell at the pump what you are really filling up with?
You may be thinking: “All I ever see are signs saying Nafta, Diesel or some premium-sounding name. How on earth am I supposed to know whether there’s a bio component in it?” The good news is that retailers are legally required to state it; it just usually isn’t in the biggest print on the advertising board.
#### Look for the B7 vs. B0 codes
Every fuel pump (and often the nozzle itself) must carry a mandatory label with an international code.
- B7: This is standard diesel, which you will find at 95% of stations. It contains up to 7% bio component (MEŘO).
- B0: This is the “holy grail”. The zero in the name means 0% bio component. If you see this label, you’re in luck: you are filling up with pure fossil diesel.
#### What about premium fuels?
“Premium diesel” is often on offer. With these fuels, it can cut both ways:
1. Some premium diesels contain a bio component, but they also contain a huge amount of additives designed to eliminate its negative effects.
1. Others use so-called HVO (hydrotreated vegetable oil) instead of rapeseed (MEŘO), a second-generation “bio” component that is chemically almost identical to pure diesel and does not cause bio sludge.
#### Ask for the “delivery note”
You have every right to! If the staff cannot tell you what is in the tank, you can ask to see the delivery note for the last delivery. It must clearly state the percentage of bio components. But let’s be honest: who wants to argue with the staff at the till? That is exactly why there is a more elegant solution.
### Chapter 5: How do you find “pure” fuel in seconds with PHMarket?
You no longer need to play detective and study delivery notes at every till. In 2026, finding quality fuel is a matter of a few taps. The PHMarket app doesn’t just track the lowest price on the price board; it acts as your personal radar for honest fuel.
#### Comparison: Is it worth paying extra?
A common myth is that bio-free diesel has to be expensive. With PHMarket you will discover that the reality is different. You will often find a station selling “pure” diesel at a lower price than standard diesel with a bio component at a motorway chain. The app works out in real time whether it is worth driving an extra two kilometres for fuel that will save your engine thousands of CZK in future repairs.
#### Peace of mind in your pocket
Using PHMarket means being in control. You no longer have to rely on chance or on what the coffee advert by the entrance tells you. You have a tool in your hand that tells you: “Fill up here, this is the fuel your engine really wants.”
Conclusion: Bio-free diesel is not just a passing fad. It is a rational choice for anyone who wants their car to serve them for a long time without breakdowns. With the PHMarket app, you can be sure you will always make this premium choice at the best possible price.
Tip for you: Before your next fill-up, open PHMarket and check whether there is a station with a B0 label near you. Your engine will thank you every time you start it.

sbohem-plastove-karticky-proc-digitalni-.title: Goodbye, plastic cards! Why is a digital price overview changing the way we fill up?
sbohem-plastove-karticky-proc-digitalni-.seoDescription: Fuel loyalty cards often don’t pay off. Find out why the PHMarket digital price overview saves you more than plastic cards ever could.
sbohem-plastove-karticky-proc-digitalni-.content:
Is your wallet bursting at the seams with loyalty cards from various fuel stations, yet you still feel you’re leaving more at the pump than you need to? You’re not alone. For years, traditional loyalty programmes taught us that collecting points for overpriced petrol is the way to save money. But let’s be honest: what good is a discount of 0.50 CZK per litre when, two streets away, fuel costs 3 CZK less even without a card? The era of collecting points and plastic cards is coming to an end. The future belongs to clean data, transparency and the freedom that the PHMarket digital overview brings.
### 1. Loyalty programmes vs. clean data: A trap for drivers?
Most loyalty programmes run by the big chains work on a simple principle: make drivers feel “special” and convinced that they are saving. Psychologically, these cards push us to keep filling up with the same brand, even when it isn’t actually the best deal for us. We become loyal to the brand, not to our own wallet.
#### Maths that doesn’t add up
Just try doing the sums. A premium fuel station on a main road charges 39.90 CZK for petrol. With a loyalty card you get a discount of 0.50 CZK per litre, so you pay 39.40 CZK. A kilometre further on, in a quieter area, there is a self-service station or a smaller local retailer charging 36.50 CZK.
Even with that “amazing” card discount, you are still overpaying by 2.90 CZK on every litre. On a 50-litre tank that comes to 145 CZK, which you have just handed over to a big chain’s marketing department in exchange for the feeling that you are collecting points towards a cuddly toy or a cheaper coffee.
#### From loyalty to being informed
The PHMarket digital overview turns this model on its head. Instead of you adapting to the petrol station, the market adapts to you. Real-time data lets you see the market as a whole, without the marketing gloss. Clean data is a far more powerful tool than any plastic loyalty programme, because it gives you what matters most: a real choice.
### 2. The power of real-time information: The end of price guesswork
Most drivers fill up out of habit. “It always used to be cheap here,” they think, and turn into the station they have known for years. But fuel prices today change dynamically, sometimes several times a day. Relying on “experience” or on what you saw on the price board yesterday morning is, these days, a sure way to overpay.
#### Why is a digital overview more accurate than the human eye?
While you concentrate on driving, PHMarket monitors the market for you. Our technology collects data from partner stations and from our community of users, creating a map that breathes in real time. You no longer have to drive around town checking the price boards of individual stations.
In a second, the app answers questions that used to take you an hour:
- Where is the nearest station of my favourite brand?
- Which station on my route currently has the lowest price?
- Is it worth filling up here, or should I drive another 10 kilometres?
#### The end of “price blindness”
Do you know that feeling when you fill the tank to the brim and, two kilometres down the road, you see a price 2 CZK lower? That is exactly what we call price blindness. A digital overview cures this blindness. Real-time information gives you a strategic advantage. Instead of hoping you are getting a good deal, with PHMarket you know.
#### Data as a quality filter
In real time we track not just the price but also relevance. If something unusual is happening on the market, such as a sudden price hike in a particular region, you will see it in the app immediately. This level of transparency used to be available only to big commodity traders. Today, thanks to PHMarket, every smartphone owner has it.
### 3. Freedom of choice: Why be a prisoner of one brand?
Many drivers suffer from what you might call “brand imprisonment”. They feel that once they have a card with one network, they have to fill up only there. But the fuel market is dynamic and no network is the cheapest always and everywhere. With PHMarket you stop being a loyal customer of one corporation and become a smart customer of the market.
#### No more dictatorship of discount tiers
Loyalty programmes often push you to fill up a certain volume to reach a better price. “Fill up 100 litres a month and get a discount,” the adverts proclaim. But that forces you to adjust your journeys and consumption to meet someone else’s conditions.
With a digital overview, these limits fall away. If today the best deal is at a local station on the edge of town and tomorrow at an automated station by the shopping centre, you simply drive there with PHMarket. You are not tied to any points, levels or stamps on a card. Your only condition is the best current balance of price and quality.
#### The power of independence
Being an independent driver means being able to use the market situation to your advantage. Local stations often react to falling oil prices far more flexibly than the big multinational giants, which take days to reset their global price lists.
Thanks to PHMarket, you see these local “price anomalies” straight away. You can support smaller, honest retailers who strive for a fair price, and save money at the same time. Freedom of choice gives you a level of control that a plastic card will never offer.
### 4. Ecology and efficiency: When less means more
It may sound like a paradox to talk about ecology in an article about combustion engines. But the least ecological (and least economical) fuel is the fuel you burn for no reason at all. How many times have you driven “to be on the safe side” to a cheaper station on the other side of town, only to find on arrival that they had already put the price up?
#### No more pointless “sightseeing tours”
In an effort to save, many drivers clock up extra kilometres hunting for a cheaper price board. Paradoxically, this wipes out the saving, wears out the car and burns extra litres. The PHMarket digital overview puts an end to this bad habit. You know exactly where you are going and why. Instead of driving round five stations, you go straight to the best-value one that happens to be on your route.
#### Time is money (literally)
Nobody will give you back the time spent pointlessly weaving through traffic to save 50 CZK. PHMarket lets you plan fill-ups as part of your normal journey. The modern driver doesn’t fill up by “searching” but by “knowing”. This efficiency saves not only your nerves and emissions in town but, above all, your precious time, which you can spend with your family or on your work.
#### A digital footprint instead of a plastic one
Getting rid of five plastic cards from your wallet is a small but symbolic step towards sustainability. Every card had to be manufactured and delivered, and one day it will end up as waste. A digital identity in the app is clean, takes up no space and you will never leave it at home on the bedside table just as the fuel warning light comes on.
### 5. How PHMarket makes life easier: Your digital co-pilot
Technology shouldn’t complicate our lives; it should spare us unnecessary decisions. PHMarket is not just a list of prices; it is an intelligent tool designed for the fast pace of 2026. Whereas you used to have to keep a “map” of cheap stations in your head, today a single tap is all you need.
#### User-friendliness first
Forget complicated searching. A good app knows what you need. PHMarket instantly shows you the best options in your immediate vicinity or on your planned route. The interface is clean and intuitive, with no pop-up adverts for baguettes, just what you care about: price, location and quality.
#### Features a plastic card can’t offer
A loyalty card won’t tell you that you are approaching a station where the price has just been updated to a record low. PHMarket will. The key benefits include:
- Navigation straight to your destination: With one tap you can link the app to your favourite navigation (Google Maps, Waze).
- Filtering by your needs: Do you specifically need diesel with additives or high-octane petrol? The app shows you only what your car really needs.
- Community updates: PHMarket gets stronger with every user. If someone spots a price change, it can show up in the app before the station owner has even had time to change the digits on the price board.
#### Everything in one place
Having a digital overview means peace of mind. You no longer have to wonder whether you have the right card for a particular network. PHMarket is a universal key to the entire market. It is the move from the chaos of countless loyalty schemes to one efficient solution that is always in your pocket.
### Conclusion: The future is digital. Are you ready?
The world around us is changing, and the way we approach buying fuel shouldn’t stay stuck in the past. The era of plastic cards and collecting points for overpriced service was merely a stepping stone to what we have today: absolute transparency. PHMarket is not just another app on your phone. It is a symbol of freedom for every driver who no longer wants to play by the rules of big corporations and would rather make decisions based on facts and up-to-date data.
Clear your wallet of unnecessary plastic and your mind of price guesswork. The future of filling up is about information, speed and fairness. And now it is literally at your fingertips.

zimni-vs-letni-nafta-co-se-skutecne-deje.title: Winter vs. summer diesel: What really happens in freezing temperatures and how to fill up correctly (2025)
zimni-vs-letni-nafta-co-se-skutecne-deje.seoDescription: The right winter diesel protects your engine in the frost. How do summer, winter and arctic diesel differ, and how can you prevent engine trouble?
zimni-vs-letni-nafta-co-se-skutecne-deje.content:
### 1. Why winter is the toughest season for diesel engines
Winter fundamentally changes the properties of fuels and materials and the way the engine works. Diesel engines are more sensitive to low temperatures than petrol engines because they rely on precise fuel metering, high pressures and fine tolerances inside the injection system. As soon as the fuel flow is disrupted, it immediately shows in starting, power and how the engine runs.
Diesel also contains natural paraffins and the mandatory bio component FAME. Both change their properties at low temperatures: paraffins crystallise, while the bio component absorbs water and can be less stable. If the fuel is old, of poor quality or unsuitable for the current season, the engine can run into trouble at temperatures of around -5 °C.
Diesel engines simply need the right fuel at the right time. And that is exactly why the difference between summer and winter diesel is crucial.
### 2. How diesel works: paraffins, the bio component and water in the fuel
Diesel is a mixture of hydrocarbons and other substances whose behaviour is governed by the laws of physics. To understand why an engine can fail in winter, it helps to know how the individual components behave.
#### Paraffins: a natural component of diesel
Paraffins give diesel its energy and lubricity. In a warm environment they are completely dissolved, but as temperatures drop they start to turn into tiny crystals. These gradually:
- increase the density of the fuel,
- reduce its fluidity,
- clog the fuel filter.
This process has its own technical parameter, CFPP (Cold Filter Plugging Point), which is the temperature at which the fuel will no longer pass through a standard filter.
#### The bio component FAME: hygroscopic and sensitive to temperature
Diesel in the EU must contain a share of the bio component FAME. It has one property that causes problems in winter: it attracts water. In cold conditions, water can:
- collect at the bottom of the tank,
- freeze in the filter,
- cause white exhaust smoke,
- impair the quality of combustion.
At the same time, the bio component naturally ages and can reduce the long-term stability of the fuel.
#### Water in the fuel
Water condensing in the tank is a common phenomenon. The less fuel there is in the tank, the more room there is for moisture. In winter this becomes a bigger problem: frozen water can block the system.
### 3. Summer vs. winter vs. arctic diesel: composition, temperature limits and standards
All types of diesel in the EU must meet the ČSN EN 590 standard, which sets out the quality requirements. The differences between the seasonal fuels, however, are fundamental.
#### Summer diesel
- used roughly from April to October,
- CFPP usually 0 to -5 °C,
- higher paraffin content,
- cheaper to produce,
- unsuitable for frosts.
Summer diesel may still work at temperatures around zero, but at -5 to -10 °C it will almost certainly start to crystallise.
#### Winter diesel
- used roughly from November to March,
- CFPP typically -15 to -20 °C,
- contains paraffin crystallisation depressants,
- tends to be more stable in terms of the bio component as well.
Winter diesel is produced by a different process or modified with special additives. So it is not marketing, but a genuine technological difference.
#### Arctic diesel
- produced for extreme conditions,
- CFPP of -30 °C or lower,
- minimal paraffin content,
- used in the mountains, in long-haul trucking or wherever severe frosts are a risk.
### 4. What happens in the fuel system in freezing temperatures
Low temperatures affect the entire fuel system:
#### Fuel filter
The first place where paraffin crystals get trapped. As soon as the filter becomes blocked, the engine does not get the amount of fuel it needs.
#### Tank
Condensation produces water, which can freeze at the bottom of the tank or in the lines.
#### High-pressure pump
It needs liquid fuel with sufficient lubricity. Thicker fuel causes greater resistance → the pump wears excessively.
#### Injectors
Blockages or poor combustion show up as rough running, jerking or a loss of power.
#### Fuel lines
Thickened diesel may flow more slowly or not at all.
The result is the classic winter failure: “the engine turns over but won’t start”.
### 5. Why summer diesel fails in winter and how you can tell
If there is summer diesel in the engine, frost causes the paraffins to crystallise rapidly. This leads to:
- poor starting or no start at all,
- an engine that fires up and immediately cuts out,
- a loss of power while driving,
- fluctuating revs,
- an irregular engine sound,
- increased smoke.
In the worst case, the car stops completely and you cannot carry on until the fuel thaws.
That is why it is important to fill up at places where the seasonal switch to winter fuel happens on time and properly.
### 6. Additives in winter: when they help and when they don’t
Diesel additives have various functions. In winter, the main ones used are:
#### Paraffin depressants
They slow down crystallisation, lower the CFPP and improve flow in frost.
#### Cetane improvers
They help with cold starts and improve combustion of the mixture.
#### Comprehensive winter additives
They combine several functions at once.
#### ❗ But one basic rule applies:
An additive helps if it is added before the problem occurs.
If the diesel has already gelled, ordinary additives will not help. Nor will they help with fuel that contains a lot of water or too high a proportion of paraffins.
Additives are therefore an excellent preventive measure, not a cure for an existing problem.
### 7. How to recognise good winter diesel and a reliable fuel station
Fuel quality is influenced by:
#### Fuel turnover
A station where people fill up frequently always has fresh fuel in its tanks. That is crucial in winter.
#### Sticking to the seasonal switch
A good station switches to winter fuel on the prescribed dates and keeps proper control over its stocks.
#### Equipment maintenance
Clean pumps, filters and tanks are a sign of a professional operation.
#### Fuel origin
Most fuel stations in the Czech Republic buy their fuel from large refineries, but the difference lies in how the fuel is handled afterwards: storage, additives and checks.
#### Transparency and stability
Stations that work with the same suppliers over the long term and run stable operations achieve better results in winter.
### 8. The most common winter problems with diesel engines and their technical causes
#### Poor cold starts
Often caused by thick fuel, a low cetane number or water in the system.
#### The engine starts and then cuts out
A typical sign of a partially clogged filter.
#### Jerking while driving
An irregular fuel supply.
#### Loss of power
The engine is not getting enough diesel.
#### White smoke
Water or condensate in the combustion chamber.
#### Noisy engine
A low cetane number or irregular combustion.
### 9. How to prevent winter problems: recommended practices
#### Fill up at stations with high turnover
Fresh fuel is crucial in winter.
#### Keep your tank at least half full
This keeps water condensation to a minimum.
#### In frosty weather, use a suitable additive as a precaution
Especially at temperatures below -10 °C.
#### Do not rely on extremely cheap fuel
A low price is not a problem in itself, but it can mean a later switch to the winter blend.
#### Fill up where they have the seasonal changeover under control
Stability and trust are key.
### 10. How PHMarket selects stations with consistent winter fuel quality
PHMarket works with fuel stations that:
- have run stable operations over the long term,
- work with vetted suppliers,
- switch to winter fuel on time,
- take good care of their equipment,
- have high fuel turnover,
- have a long track record of trouble-free fill-ups.
The aim is not to rate fuel quality by its content, because within the ČSN EN 590 standard that is the same for all suppliers, but to give drivers the certainty that they are filling up at a place where seasonal preparation, logistics and operations are genuinely under control.
All of this increases the chance that your engine will run reliably even in harder frosts.
## Conclusion
Winter places high demands on both diesel engines and fuel. The difference between summer, winter and arctic diesel is not cosmetic: these are technological differences that have a major impact on starting, the combustion process and the overall reliability of the engine. The right winter diesel, good maintenance, fresh fuel and preventive measures can prevent most of the problems that would otherwise mean high repair costs.
Filling up at verified stations is not only safer but also more economical in the long run.
And that is exactly why PHMarket connects drivers with fuel stations that have their seasonal preparation under control and offer consistent quality of service, so that every kilometre is safer, more reliable and cheaper.
